newsitem.title: KUWAIT: U.S. says Iraq unlikely to provoke new attacks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says Iraq unlikely to provoke new attacks.

text.p: The United States said on Sunday that Iraqi President Saddam Hussein seemed unlikely to provoke a renewed attack by U.S. forces and after a peaceful weekend tensions in the Gulf appeared to cool.

The U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, Madeleine Albright, said in a television interview: "We are not going to be pressed into overreacting...It looks as though Saddam Hussein is not going to do anything else."
Iraq said on Friday it would no longer fire anti-aircraft missiles at U.S. and allied warplanes enforcing "no-fly" zones in northern and southern Iraq.

Pressed on whether it would take another provocation for the United States to renew the attacks it unleashed this month after an Iraqi-backed onslaught on one Kurdish faction, Albright said: "I think we're going to keep watching the whole issue very, very carefully."

"We want to make sure that our pilots are safe and that the no-fly zone is something that we can maintain," she added. The United States and its allies set up "no-fly" zones in Iraq's north and south after the 1991 Gulf War.

On Sunday, the Pentagon delayed plans for the possible deployment of up to 5,000 additional Army troops to join a U.S. buildup in and around the Gulf, apparently because of Kuwaiti qualms about being host to them.

"Because the situation is ever-changing, it seems they may or may not ever be utilised," said Navy Lt. Cmdr. Scott Campbell, a Pentagon spokesman. The troops from Fort Hood in Texas had been alerted on Friday night for possible deployment to the Gulf on Sunday.

U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry, shuttling between Gulf allies and Turkey to consult on Iraq policy, said he had asked Kuwait's emir, Sheikh Jaber al-Ahmad al-Sabah, for permission to deploy 5,000 U.S. troops in the Gulf state.
He has also ordered a battery of Scud-busting Patriot missiles to Kuwait to strengthen its air defences.
Asked if more U.S. strikes against Iraq were still possible, Perry told a news conference on a brief visit to Kuwait: "Yes, it is still a possibility."

The United States "will take whatever action is necessary" to enforce an expanded southern Iraqi no-fly zone up to the 33rd parallel, which runs 50 km (30 miles) south of Baghdad, and to protect the pilots who patrol it.
Perry said that Iraq had fired a total of six missiles at U.S. planes during this month's conflict.

The latest crisis between the United States and Iraq started 15 days ago. Washington punished Iraq for intervening in the faction fighting in its Kurdish north by launching cruise missiles at air defence systems in southern Iraq.

Kuwait, grateful to the United States for leading the 1991 Gulf War that liberated it from a seven-month Iraqi occupation, is so far the only Arab country to support Washington in its latest standoff with Saddam.
But Kuwaiti Foreign Minister Sheikh Sabah al-Ahmad al-Jaber al-Sabah said on Sunday there was no question of U.S. land forces crossing into Iraq from Kuwait.
Russia repeated its criticism of Washington's approach. A Baghdad-based diplomat went as far as saying that Iraq had a right to shoot down planes in the no-fly zones.
"When they have warplanes of another country flying over their airspace they have the right to shoot," Vladimir Titorenko of the Russian mission in Baghdad told Reuters in an interview.
Iraq stepped up its criticism of the United States.

The government newspaper al-Jumhouriya, which said on Saturday it hoped the decision to suspend missile attacks would ease tension in the Gulf, on Sunday attacked Clinton in some of the strongest language ever used by Iraq against a U.S. leader.
"He is mentally retarded, immersed in vice and without conscience," said a front-page editorial.

The Arab League, which groups all Arabs states including Iraq and Washington's close allies in the Gulf, condemned U.S. cruise missile attacks on Iraq earlier this month, saying they violated Iraqi sovereignty.
While most of its regional allies are unwilling to take part, Washington has pressed on with the buildup in the region, including sending a second aircraft carrier battle group.
The U.S. aircraft carrier Enterprise, with about 75 warplanes on board, steamed out of the Suez Canal and into the Red Sea en route to the Gulf.

As the United States pushed ahead with its military buildup in the Gulf, its Kurdish allies in northern Iraq began crossing into Turkey to escape the wrath of Saddam. Hundreds of Kurds clutching suitcases crossed the Turkish border, witnesses said.
